subject: bayesplot - model comparisons + multiple summaries vs x?

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: bayesplot - model comparisons + multiple summaries vs x?
parts:
Hi!

First I have to say that the more I look into bayesplot the more amazed I am, this package is great!

When going over the functions I could not find two things which would be nice to do (but maybe its there and I haven't seen it):

- Model comparisons? Can these be done? Side-by-side predictive comparisons would be great. Should I do that with the superimposing functions or is there more to come?

- Can I plot something what people in the modeling community call visual predictive checks (VPC)? The idea is that a model is built for some data y which is regressed against a continuous x. Assume that x is measured at fixed points x_1, x_2, ... Now what I would like to plot is some summary statistic at each x_1, x_2, ... at each time-point and the plot it against x. This is done as usual for the actual data and for each replicated data set. The summary statistics are often quantiles (10%, 50% and 90%) and I would like to have all three of these shown in the plot. On top of that I often have groupings in my data for which I want to split this plot. Is this doable with bayesplot already?

Many thanks!

Best,
Sebastian

Even though there's already a lot in the package I'm really just getting started with it. Plots for comparing models like this are high on my to-do list. If you have any specific suggestions about what they should look like, the feedback is more than welcome!

- Can I plot something what people in the modeling community call visual predictive checks (VPC)? The idea is that a model is built for some data y which is regressed against a continuous x. Assume that x is measured at fixed points x_1, x_2, ... Now what I would like to plot is some summary statistic at each x_1, x_2, ... at each time-point and the plot it against x. This is done as usual for the actual data and for each replicated data set. The summary statistics are often quantiles (10%, 50% and 90%) and I would like to have all three of these shown in the plot. On top of that I often have groupings in my data for which I want to split this plot. Is this doable with bayesplot already?

I'd like to add a lot more flexibility for this but, if I understand correctly, I think something along these lines can already be done with ppc_intervals and ppc_ribbon. There are also versions of both of those functions that end in the suffix _grouped that allow you to pass a vector of group indices to split the observations/predictions into groups. 
 
Jonah

messages.subject: Re: bayesplot - model comparisons + multiple summaries vs x?
parts:
Hi!

No really, I am very happy with things so far. I maintain a package myself which uses Stan in the backend and I want to bridge it to bayesplot. I am still not 100% whats best here. The way rstanarm has done is it supercool as it gives a huge flexibility. However, the example given in the vignette would give my package a very limited pp_check. Not yet sure whats best (mimic stanreg objects maybe and use rstanarm?).

I hate adding more dependencies to packages I write for obvious reasons, but bayesplot and rstantools will be an exception to that rule to minimize depedencies.

I will look into ppc_interval as you suggest shortly and let you now.

A thought for model comparison: Why not make yrep an array with one more dimension where the extra dimension is over the different models. Then you could use the existing ppc functions which are then generalized to multiple yreps and this implies an automatic grouping which is used to plot things side-by-side? This is an unfinished thought, but maybe worth following up.

Sebastian

parts:
Hi Jonah!

I checked out intervals and ribbon (and their grouped versions), but I haven't found a way to accomplish what I am looking for. Attached is an example VPC along with a script to generate it for the mtcars data set. Did I overlook a function in bayesplot or could this be a potential plot for bayesplot?

I find the plot quite useful. Although one has to say that the most commonly raised criticism is that one has a need for binning which forces one to put things into the bin which may have vastly different covariates. Splitting the dataset into more homogeneous subset improves this, but then the bins get a small number of entries only.

The way I used to code the VPC can certainly be improved, but I am curious what you think.

Best,
Sebastian
